extracted.intended_audience: general readers, law students, journalists and practitioners seeking comparative defamation law guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative legal standards and substantive criteria used across jurisdictions to define, prove, defend against, and punish defamation (civil and criminal), including elements of the cause of action, available defences, corporate-plaintiff rules, and online/publication rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: General common-law elements of defamation (common law provinces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation covers any communication that tends to lower the esteem of the subject in the minds of ordinary members of the public; intent is presumed and it is not necessary to prove that the defendant intended to defame; as the law assumes that an individual suffers loss if a statement is defamatory, there is no need to prove specific damage or loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant may avail themselves of defences such as justification (the truth), fair comment, responsible communication, or privilege. Publishers may use innocent dissemination where they had no knowledge of the nature of the statement, it was not brought to their attention, and they were not negligent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil defamation ingredients (Australian summary per Duffy v Google)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tort can be divided into the following ingredients: the defendant participates in publication to a third party of a body of work; the body of work contains a passage alleged to be defamatory; the passage conveys an imputation; the imputation is about the plaintiff; the imputation is damaging to the plaintiff's reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available defences include absolute privilege, qualified privilege, justification (truth), honest opinion, publication of public documents, fair report of proceedings of public concern and triviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences to defamation (general list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common defences across jurisdictions include justification (truth), fair comment/honest opinion, responsible communication (on matters of public interest), privilege (absolute and qualified), innocent dissemination, triviality, publication of public documents, and fair report of proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some defences have jurisdiction-specific limits (e.g., truth may be unavailable in certain private-life contexts in France). Malice can negate some defences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate-plaintiff limitations (jurisdictional variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdictions differ on corporate ability to sue: Australian law (contemporary) generally denies private corporations the right to sue for defamation except small businesses; Canadian law grants private corporations substantially the same right as individuals; English law (since 2013) allows private corporations to sue but requires proof that the defamation caused serious harm and serious financial loss; Section 6 (Canada) allows corporate actions only when pecuniary loss is alleged and proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where corporations are restricted, they may still pursue alternative torts (e.g., injurious falsehood) which require different proof (economic loss and malice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actio iniuriarum elements (Roman-Dutch and Scots law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability under the actio iniuriarum requires harm (infringement of a personality interest: corpus, dignitas, or fama), wrongful conduct, and intention; causation is often assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because dignitas is wide, its infringement must be serious (contumelia). For non-patrimonial interests, Scots law requires deliberate affront (animus iniuriandi); negligent interference is insufficient to generate liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contumelia / deliberate affront requirement (Scots/actio context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct must be 'contumelious'—showing hubristic disregard of the pursuer's personality interest such that an intention to affront can be imputed; negligent interference with a non-patrimonial interest will not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This raises a higher threshold than mere negligence; intent (or imputed intent) is central in this strand of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal defamation (existence and typical features)
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to tort law, many jurisdictions treat defamation as a criminal offence with penalties; criminal defamation provisions vary by country and may include special offences for defaming authorities or public figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human-rights groups often critique criminal defamation as restricting freedom of expression; international bodies (e.g., European Court of Human Rights) have placed limits on criminal libel laws. Penalties and scope differ widely by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group libel principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, group libel required statements to 'descend to particulars' to be actionable against identifiable individuals; some cases treated publications defaming a whole community as libel if the publication implied acts common to the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group libel was often criminalized historically because of the risk of breach of the peace; modern treatment varies by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet publication and jurisdiction (Dow Jones v Gutnick principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet-published foreign publications that defame an Australian in their Australian reputation can be held accountable under Australian defamation law; online publication raises jurisdiction and limitation-period questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This case is often cited for the principle that publication occurs where material is downloaded/read; other jurisdictions have different approaches. Note also that the Supreme Court of Canada held posting hyperlinks to defamatory content is not itself publication for libel purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of libel/slander distinction (Australia 2006 reforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform defamation laws in Australia abolished the distinction between libel and slander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms also introduced new defences (e.g., triviality) and restricted corporate rights to sue; truth became an unqualified defence (defendant must prove imputations substantially true).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triviality defence (Australia 2006 reforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defence to the publication of a defamatory matter exists if the defendant proves the circumstances of publication were such that the plaintiff was unlikely to sustain any harm (triviality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits suits over publications unlikely to have caused reputational harm; malice can negate defences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth/justification defence with limits (France and other jurisdictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: France provides truth as the principal statutory defence, but it is unavailable in cases involving an individual's personal life; French courts recognize exceptions (references over ten years old, pardoned/expunged records, and a plea of good faith under specified criteria).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good faith defence factors: pursues a legitimate aim; not driven by animosity/malice; is prudent and measured; is backed by a serious investigation that dutifully sought to ascertain the truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quebec civil defamation standard (reasonableness approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Quebec (Civil Code), to establish civil liability the plaintiff must show injury (fault), a wrongful act (damage), and causal connection; defamation in Quebec is governed by a reasonableness standard rather than strict liability—defendant will not be held liable if it was reasonable to believe the statement was true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with strict-liability approaches elsewhere and focuses on whether the defendant's belief and conduct were reasonable under the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal libel / libel known to be false (Canada)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal Code of Canada defines 'defamatory libel' and criminalizes 'libel known to be false' as an indictable offence with a maximum prison term of five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal prosecutions for defamation in Canada have been rare; criminal libel often arises against agents of the Crown; statistics show limited prosecutions and convictions historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: China — statutory personality-rights framework and enforcement tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Chinese Civil Code (Personality Rights) recognizes reputation, honour, privacy and dignity; provides liability for fabrication, distortion, lack of verification, misrepresentation and offers rights to request correction or deletion; Criminal Law Article 246 punishes serious defamation with up to three years' imprisonment or criminal detention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil provisions include factors for verification considerations such as source credibility, controversial information, timeliness, public order and morals, and special rules for depictions in artistic works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction-specific definitions and penalties (survey entries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various countries define defamation/calumny/injury differently and set differing penalties (fines, imprisonment, aggravated penalties for public or group defamation, enhanced penalties for defaming authorities or committing defamation in public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Argentina (calumny vs injury distinctions, fines), Austria (specific criminal code provisions), Azerbaijan (large fines and possible imprisonment), Belgium (distinction between calumny and defamation with imprisonment/fines and aggravated penalties for motive of hatred), Brazil (different classifications: defamation, calumny, injury with varied penalties), Bulgaria (criminal offence but imprisonment removed), Finland (defamation versus dissemination of information violating privacy), and others. Each jurisdiction may also have exemptions (e.g., Croatia's exemption for scientific, literary, journalistic contexts provided conduct was not aimed at harming reputation).

rubrics_metrics.name: India — statutory definition and procedural constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Indian Penal Code (Section 499, now replaced by Section 356 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita), defamation is defined as making or publishing any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm the person's reputation, with ten exceptions; punishment up to two years imprisonment or fine or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal defamation in India is prosecuted only upon complaint (within six months) per the Code of Criminal Procedure; related offences and exceptions (e.g., insults against religion, public servants) interact with defamation provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finland — privacy-sensitive dissemination offence
rubrics_metrics.description: Finnish law criminalizes defamation (spreading a false report or insinuation apt to cause harm) and also criminalizes 'dissemination of information violating personal privacy' which can apply even to accurate information if disseminated in a way apt to harm someone's right to privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information relevant to public office, business conduct, or public interest is not covered by the privacy dissemination prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions for protected contexts (e.g., Croatia, scholarly/journalistic works)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions exempt statements made in scientific work, literary or artistic works, public information by politicians/government officials, journalistic work, or defence of a right, provided the conduct was not aimed at damaging someone's reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exemptions recognize public-interest or expressive contexts but require an absence of malicious intent to apply.
